passage: Thursday after school, outside the tuition centre in the colony, Kabir tapped his phone. "We're all bunking. Mall, then the arcade. Uday, you in? Or are you going to run to tuition like a good boy?" A couple of them smirked. Uday's chest went tight. He didn't want to go; he had a test the next day. But the thought of the group chat filling with jokes about him made his mouth say, "Yeah, sure." At the mall he kept checking the time and laughed a beat too late at everything. That night he admitted to himself that he had been scared, plain and simple. Next day he told Harsha, who groaned, "Me too. I hate saying no." They practised at lunch: "Nah, I'll pass, catch you later." It sounded clumsy and easy at once.

qa.q: Where did the group go after Kabir said they were bunking?
qa.a: To the mall and then the arcade.

qa.q: Why did Uday say yes even though he didn't want to go?
qa.a: He was afraid of being laughed at and left out. His chest went tight and he imagined the group chat filling with jokes about him.

qa.q: What small steps did Uday take to handle the pressure next time?
qa.a: He admitted the fear was real, found Harsha as an ally who would say no with him, and practised a short reply like "Nah, I'll pass, catch you later."

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Uday admitted his fear?
qa.a: Relieved. Harsha groaned and said "Me too," which suggests the same fear of saying no and gladness at not being alone.

grounding: The protagonist goes along out of fear of ridicule, then admits the fear, finds an ally and practises a short reply.

passage:
"Sangeeta, you're coming, right? We're all bunking the last period to go to the lake."
"Um… yeah. Sure."
Later, by the lockers:
"Arohi, can I tell you something? I don't actually want to go."
"Then why did you say yes?"
"Because if I don't, they'll laugh and call me a goody-goody. And then they'll go without me every time."
"That's a real fear. I have it too."
"You do?"
"I also don't want to go. My mum would kill me, and honestly the lake gets scary at that end."
"So… what if we both say no? Together?"
"Okay. What do we say?"
"Something short. Like, 'Not today, we've got a project.'"
"'Not today, we've got a project.' Say it again."
"Not today, we've got a project."
They practised it twice, giggling. When Riya came back to check, Sangeeta said it first, steady, though her hands were cold. Arohi nodded beside her. Riya shrugged. "Your loss." And that was all.

qa.q: Where were the friends planning to go during the last period?
Why did Sangeeta first say yes?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at, called a goody-goody and left out of future plans.

qa.q: What helped Sangeeta say no, and why?
qa.a: Finding an ally in Arohi and practising a short reply together made it easier to refuse calmly.

qa.q: How does Riya react to the refusal?
qa.a: Riya just shrugs and says 'Your loss,' showing the feared reaction was much smaller than Sangeeta expected.

grounding: A teen who goes along out of fear of being left out admits the fear, finds an ally and practises a short reply.

passage:
Last year my friends started bunking Saturday tuition to hang around the arcade. The first week, I went. The second week too. I didn't even enjoy it. I kept checking the time and feeling guilty about the money Papa paid for tuition.
I went because I was scared. Scared they'd laugh, scared I'd be the one left out of every photo in the group.
One Saturday I noticed Yash was quiet too. On the walk, I asked him, "Do you actually want to be here?" He said, "Not at all." We both laughed, a bit shakily.
So we made a plan. We practised one line in his building's lift: "We're doing tuition today, see you after." Short. Boring. No speech.
The next Saturday we said it together. Someone called us nerds. That was it.
I'm Omkar, and what I learned is that fear doesn't disappear. It just gets smaller when someone stands next to you.

qa.q: Where were Omkar's friends going instead of tuition?
Why did Omkar keep going along with the group?
qa.a: Omkar felt scared of being laughed at and left out, even while feeling guilty and not enjoying it.

qa.q: What small step helped Omkar stop, and why?
qa.a: Finding Yash as an ally and practising one short line made it easier to say no together.

qa.q: How did Yash feel about bunking tuition?
qa.a: Yash felt the same unease, not wanting to be there at all, and was relieved to find someone who felt the same.

grounding: A teen who goes along out of fear admits it, finds an ally who will say no too, and practises a short reply.
